segments.text: Welcome to Staff Coders Fast API
learning module, error handling. Today,
we'll learn how Fast API reports what
went wrong using a bike rental service
as our example. Things go wrong on
purpose. A bike that doesn't exist, a
bike someone else is riding, a rental of
48 hours when the limit is 24. None of
those are bugs. They're answers. The
question is how your service gives them
with the right code in the same shape
every time. Failures aren't bugs.
They're answers. Picture the rental
service with no plan for failure. The
root calls a service function, which
calls the store. Three levels deep, the
bike turns out to be taken. Now what?
Return none and the root has to notice.
Return an error dict and the root has to
check for it. Raise your own exception
and nobody catches it. The caller gets a
500 and you get a stack trace.
Meanwhile, validation errors come back
in Fast API's shape, not yours. So
clients parse two formats. Every
failure, a different shape. Every
caller, confused. Here's the model. An
exception raised anywhere below your
root climbs back up through every call
until something catches it. Fast API
catches at the top. An HTTP exception is
the simplest case. Raise it three levels
deep and Fast API turns it into the
reply you described,
404 with the detail. For your own
failures, an exception handler is a
function you register once on the app.
This exception type, this reply. Every
time that type climbs out of any root,
the handler answers. The framework's own
validation error is just another type,
so it can get a handler, too. Raise it
deep, answer it once. Let's build it. In
services.py,
start rental. Look up the bike. If it's
missing, raise HTTP exception 404 bike
not found. If it's taken, we'll come
back to that. Mark it rented and return
the rental. In the router, at
router.post/rentals
status code 201, def create rental and
return start rental with the bike ID. No
try, no if. Send bike 7, 201 rented.
Send bike 99, 404 bike not found. The
raise happened in the service, two calls
down. The route never saw it. Fast API
answered. Raise in the service, Fast API
replies. Next level. Bike 12 exists, but
it's out with someone. That's not a 404
and it isn't Fast API's business. It's
ours. Class bike unavailable exception,
remembering the bike ID. In the service,
if the bike is rented, raise bike
unavailable. Send bike 12, 500. Nothing
caught it. So teach the app in main.py
at app.exception_handler
bike unavailable, def bike unavailable
with the request and the exception.
Build one body shape, error code
message. Return a JSON response status
code 409 conflict. Send it again, 409
and the message names bike 12. One raise
anywhere, one answer here. Now the
framework's own report. Send 48 hours,
422 in Fast API's shape, detail loc msg.
Register a handler for request value
value and reshape it. The same envelope,
code invalid request and the field names
pulled out of loc. Send it again, 422
our shape, fields hours. Last, give HTTP
exception the same treatment. So, the
404 wears the envelope, too. Now, every
refusal has one shape, one handler per
failure, one envelope for all. Here's
the one that looks responsible. Someone
wraps the service call in try except
bike unavailable and returns a dict.
Error, bike unavailable. Send bike 12,
201 created, and the body says error.
The status says it worked. The body says
it didn't. A client that checks the code
now thinks it has a bike. The root
caught the failure and turned it into a
success. The fix is a deletion. Remove
the try. Let the exception climb. The
handler was waiting for it. Send it
again. 409 in the envelope. Don't catch
it. Let it climb. Let's recap. An
exception raised anywhere below the root
climbs up to FastAPI. HTTP exception
becomes the reply you described. A
custom exception is your own failure
with its own class. An exception
handler, registered once on the app,
answers one type everywhere. Request
value value can be reshaped the same
way, and one envelope keeps every
refusal in one shape. Now, your
challenge. A scooter sharing app
registers one exception handler for its
own scooter offline exception, returning
a 409 envelope. A root raises HTTP
exception 404 scooter not found. Who
answers? A, the scooter offline handler
with a 409. B, FastAPI's default with a
404 and a detail. C, nobody, so a 500.
The answer is in the description.
Practice it on the FastAPI [music] path.
Click the link in the description. If
this helped, like, share, and subscribe.
